entries.text: That we are loosing all contacts to the real world while replacing it with a digital one we hope will give us happiness and meaning. My interests is a mix of fighting and documenting this reality.

When it comes to the future of art universities, I am concerned with the political changes that are increasing the pressure on the artistic sector to justify their raison d’être. As agents and pioneers of social change, art universities will continue to play a central role in society in the future – perhaps an even greater one – whilst at the same time facing increasing pressure to justify their existence and secure their funding. In the newly created university developement unit, we focus on how the contexts in which artists work are set to change, how art and artificial intelligence complement one another, and what impact this will have on curricula and learning outcomes.
unpredictability in general

I'm interested in highlighting knowledge that connects people across cultures, disciplines, and perspectives.

I find the question almost impossibly open. As everything I will do lies in the future, everything I do is of interest regarding the future. When thinking about what the future might hold for myself, my colleagues, my students, my field, I am interested in/concerned about how AI will influence creative practices and our perception of the world: How will we regard and perceive information, creativity, originality, contribution, usefulness, human(?) expression, empathy? I have many of the same concerns in connection to the relentlessly increasing dominance of social media. In a world of continuous posing and individualism, what does it mean to be a community? What does it mean to collaborate, to be useful, to contribute? What will it mean to linger, to take time, to reflect, to be slow?  I am also very concerned with how the arts will be perceived in times of conflict, war, climate change, far-right extremism. How can our fields articulate and argue for our (obvious) relevance in creating and maintaining solid democracies and healthy societies?

Looking to the near future (5-10 years), I am interested in the direction we as humanity are heading, as reflected in the choices we make. Do we choose out of fear, trying to preserve and control what we know and 'own', or do we dare to embrace this liminal time, embracing the unknown, insecurity and working together to explore and shape our future? As humanity, we are capable of destroying the world; will we acknowledge this and make the choice to recognise that the world can only continue to exist if we choose to be hopeful and caring. I love the new generation that we are educating, it is up to them to see new futures. It is up to us to help the transition. I am curious to see new futures arising and look forward to shape them together with all living.  Translated with DeepL.com (free version)

Rather than treating foresight as a separate activity, we are embedding it into our regular quality and governance processes. We are developing a quality architecture that combines continuous monitoring, quality dialogues and periodic programme reviews with dedicated future-oriented activities. These include regular future workshops, systematic scanning for weak signals, the establishment of a strategic observatory, and ongoing engagement with key stakeholder groups—including students, graduates, academic staff and external partners—to better understand changing expectations, needs and emerging opportunities. Collaboration is central to this approach. We deliberately bring together different perspectives and combine institutional data with qualitative insights and external developments. Our aim is to foster an institutional culture in which asking “What is changing, and what does this mean for us?” becomes a regular leadership practice. We see quality management, Institutional Research and foresight as complementary functions that strengthen the university’s capacity to learn, adapt and shape its future proactively.

On a strategic level, my institution performs a yearly internal control, a sort of SWOT analysis, with focus on W and T, where we assess potential risks of potential developments. My institution has established several courses in digital media and AI, as well as a series of AI seminars. All faculties have or are about to develop guidelines for use of AI. For our study programs (BA, MA, PhD), we have program committees and program leaders responsible for looking ahead and undertake quality assurance measurements, which e.g. might include adapting course descriptions, exam forms and evaluation criteria to the emerging technologies. More importantly, we participate in significant research projects and research centers revolving around new technologies, particularly AI, as well as research on climate change and digital changes.
